title: Everyday Situations: Choose What Happens Next
summary: Four common adult situations about work pressure, family expectations, money worries and repairing after a conflict. The client chooses, sees what might happen, and the psychologist leads the discussion.
clinicianNotes: Scenarios are original conversation starters, not a measure of mental health. Every option has a realistic consequence and none is shameful. Draft content: needs review by a licensed psychologist and a cultural fit check before use with patients.

scenarios.title: The late request
scenarios.story: Just as you are about to leave, your manager asks for a big report by tomorrow morning. You already worked late twice this week and feel your shoulders tightening. What do you do?

options.text: Explain what you can realistically finish tonight, and agree a clear deadline for the rest.
options.outcome: Your manager pauses, then agrees to a revised plan. You leave on time with a clear head.
options.note: Names limits and offers a solution. Explore what made it possible and what makes it hard in other settings.

options.text: Say yes and stay late again without saying how you feel.
options.outcome: The report is done, but you go home exhausted and quietly resentful.
options.note: Compliance avoids conflict but costs energy. Explore fears about saying no.

options.text: Snap that this is unfair and leave without finishing.
options.outcome: The tension rises and the next morning is awkward with everyone.
options.note: Anger often follows long suppression. Explore what built up before this moment.

scenarios.keyMessage: Clear, calm limits protect both health and work. Saying what is possible is not the same as refusing.
scenarios.discussion: What is one sentence you could use the next time work asks for more than you can give?

scenarios.title: The family gathering
scenarios.story: An older relative says in front of everyone that you should have settled down or earned more by now. Others nod. You feel your face go hot. What do you do?

options.text: Stay calm, thank them for caring, and say you are making your own choices at your own pace.
options.outcome: A few people look surprised, but the conversation moves on. You feel steadier afterwards.
options.note: Respectful boundary with family. Explore how this fits the person's values and culture.

options.text: Smile, say nothing, and replay it in your head for days.
options.outcome: The gathering stays peaceful, but the comment keeps echoing and your mood drops.
options.note: Silence keeps peace but the feeling stays inside. Explore what would feel safe to say.

options.text: Argue back in front of everyone.
options.outcome: The room goes quiet and the argument is remembered longer than the comment.
options.note: Strong reactions often come from hurt or shame. Explore what was underneath.

scenarios.keyMessage: You can honour family and still hold your own boundaries. Respect works in both directions.
scenarios.discussion: Whose opinion about your life weighs most on you, and what do you want them to understand?

scenarios.title: The unexpected bill
scenarios.story: A large bill arrives that you did not plan for. Your partner asks what is wrong. You feel ashamed and your stomach drops. What do you do?

options.text: Tell your partner the truth and sit down together to look at options.
options.outcome: It is uncomfortable, but you feel relief. Together you find a plan for the next months.
options.note: Shares the burden and problem-solves. Explore what makes money talk difficult.

options.text: Say it is nothing and worry alone through the night.
options.outcome: You avoid a hard conversation, but sleep is poor and the worry grows.
options.note: Hiding worries often increases them. Explore shame and what the person fears might happen.

options.text: Spend on something to feel better and avoid thinking about it.
options.outcome: The relief lasts an evening. The bill is still there and now so is the guilt.
options.note: Avoidance spending is a coping attempt. Explore what the person needs when stressed.

scenarios.keyMessage: Money worries shrink when shared. Facing the problem early gives more choices.
scenarios.discussion: Who could you tell about a money worry, and what would help you start that talk?

scenarios.title: After the argument
scenarios.story: You had a sharp argument with someone close. Today you are both being silent and the house feels heavy. What do you do?

options.text: Say you did not like how it ended, that you want to understand each other, and ask when to talk.
options.outcome: They are relieved you spoke first. You both listen better than the night before.
options.note: Takes the first step to repair. Explore what the person needs to feel safe repairing.

options.text: Wait and hope it blows over.
options.outcome: The silence drags on, and small things start feeling tense.
options.note: Waiting avoids risk but also repair. Explore the fear behind waiting.

options.text: Send a cutting message or give the silent treatment until they apologise.
options.outcome: The distance grows and both of you feel more alone.
options.note: Punishing silence usually protects hurt pride. Explore what the person hoped the other would see.

scenarios.keyMessage: Repair matters more than who was right. A first step does not mean giving in.
scenarios.discussion: What helps you feel ready to talk after a difficult argument?
